title: Horses from Egypt, a Fire in Zion
sum: The fifth of Isaiah's six woes again condemns Judah's leaders for running to Egypt for horses and chariots while they ignore the Holy One of Israel. Egypt is human, not God; when the LORD stretches out his hand, helper and helped fall together. Then the picture turns: like a lion that will not let go of its prey, and like birds hovering over a nest, the LORD of Armies will guard Jerusalem, pass over it and rescue it.

The chapter ends with a call to return to the LORD and throw away idols, and a promise that Assyria will fall to a sword that no man holds. Chapter 37 tells how that happened. The LORD who does this has his fire in Zion: his presence protects the city and threatens all who oppose him.
readings: Read as a political sermon

Isaiah speaks to a court that is negotiating with the Cushite pharaohs of Egypt in about 703–701 BC. His argument is practical as well as religious: Egypt will not save you, and trusting it means breaking faith with the LORD, who alone decides what happens to Zion.
Read as a promise woven into a warning

The lion of 31:4 at first seems to threaten Zion, and the birds of 31:5 to protect it. Many readers see the chapter as a model of the whole of Isaiah 28–33: judgment on Jerusalem's leaders, then a sudden turn to rescue, so that Zion is saved by God and not by its own plans.

views.H: The setting is Hezekiah's revolt against Sennacherib. Egypt did send an army in 701, and Sennacherib says he defeated it at Eltekeh. The promise that Assyria would fall without a human sword is told as fulfilled in 37:36, when the Assyrian army withdrew from Jerusalem.
views.C: Most scholars assign 31:1–3 to Isaiah in the years before 701. Many think 31:5–9, with the promise of rescue and the call to repent, was shaped or added later, in Josiah's time or after, when Jerusalem's escape in 701 was seen as proof that the LORD defends Zion. Others defend the unity of the chapter.
views.J: Rashi and Radak read the chapter of Hezekiah's day and of Sennacherib's defeat. The Passover verb in 31:5 (pasach) let later tradition join the rescue of Jerusalem to the night of the exodus, so that Sennacherib's army falls on Passover night in the Haggadah's poems.
views.X: Christian readers have heard in 31:5 the God who shelters his people like a bird, the picture Jesus uses over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37). The contrast of flesh and spirit in 31:3 became a classic text against trusting human power instead of God.
views.F: Some futurist readers see in the LORD coming down to fight on Mount Zion (31:4) a pattern for a last battle for Jerusalem, when the nations gather against it and the LORD defends it (Zechariah 14:2–4). Most read the chapter as fulfilled in 701.

deep.b:
For this part the translator read these witnesses directly, verse by verse: the Hebrew of the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), word by word, as edited in STEPBible's TAHOT with its Ketiv and Qere notes; the Dead Sea scrolls that preserve these chapters, in the transcription of Martin Abegg, James Bowley and Edward Cook (ETCBC), namely the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) for every verse, and 1Q8 (1QIsa-b), 4Q55, 4Q56 and 4Q57 where they survive; and the Greek in Swete's edition, which prints mostly Codex Vaticanus. For chapters 36–39 the Hebrew of Isaiah was compared word by word with 2 Kings 18:13–20:19.

Everything else is reported from the editions and studies named in each entry: the critical Greek of Ziegler's Göttingen edition, the Latin Vulgate, the Targum and the Syriac; the physical state of the scrolls (corrections, margins and blank lines), from the official edition by Eugene Ulrich and Peter Flint (DJD 32) and the studies cited; and the Assyrian records, from their published editions.

echoes: Isaiah 30:1–7; Isaiah 36:6–9; Deuteronomy 17:16; Psalm 20:7; Exodus 12:13; Matthew 23:37; Isaiah 37:36; Isaiah 29:1–8; Jeremiah 17:5

settings.what: The woe on the Egyptian alliance
settings.to: Hezekiah's court and the war party in Jerusalem
settings.when: about 703–701 BC, as envoys go to Egypt to arrange help against Assyria, or (for some) the Ashdod revolt of 713–711
settings.why: To shame the planners who trust chariots and ignore the LORD, and to warn that Egypt and Judah will fall together. Knowing the hearers were the king's own advisers makes the dry "he too is wise" (31:2) a direct jab at their pride.
views: Most date chapters 30–31 to Hezekiah's revolt against Sennacherib.
Some date them to the Ashdod revolt, when Judah also looked to Egypt (compare chapter 20).

settings.what: The lion and the birds: the LORD will guard Zion
settings.by: Isaiah, reporting what the LORD said to him
settings.to: the people of Jerusalem under the Assyrian threat
settings.when: the same crisis, or (for many critical scholars) a later reshaping of Isaiah's words after Jerusalem's escape
settings.why: To promise that the LORD, not Egypt, will defend the city, and to call the people to turn back to him and throw away their idols. The call to return in 31:6–7 makes rescue and repentance belong together.
views: Isaiah himself turns from judgment to promise in the crisis of 701, as in 29:5–8.
Editors in Josiah's time or later added the promise, reading the events of 701 back into Isaiah's warning.

title: A King Who Rules Rightly
sum: Chapter 32 opens with a short portrait of good government. A king will reign for righteousness and his officials for justice; each will be shelter from wind and rain and shade in a dry land. The blindness and deafness God laid on the people (6:10) will be lifted, and words will match reality again: no one will call a godless fool noble or a crook a great man.

Then the prophet turns to the carefree women of Jerusalem: within a little over a year the harvest will fail, and they will mourn as the palace and city are abandoned. The ruin lasts until a spirit is poured out from on high. Then the wilderness becomes garden land, justice and righteousness settle there, and righteousness yields peace and safety forever.
readings: Read as wisdom about rulers

Verses 1–8 sound like Proverbs: the noble and the fool, the shelter good rulers give, the deceit of the crook. Read this way, the passage describes what a just government is like, in any age, and holds Judah's leaders to it.
Read as messianic hope

Read beside 9:6–7 and 11:1–9, the king of 32:1 is the coming son of David, and the spirit of 32:15 is God's gift in the last days. Jewish and Christian interpreters alike have read the chapter as a picture of the age to come.

views.H: The just king is most naturally Hezekiah or a king like him, set against the corrupt court of the years before 701. The warning to the women fits the invasion of 701, which stripped the land of a year's harvest (37:30).
views.C: Many scholars treat 32:1–8 as a wisdom poem added to the book, dating it to Josiah's time (Hermann Barth) or after the exile. Verses 9–14 are widely held to be Isaiah's, and 32:15–20 a later promise that turns his warning into hope.
views.J: Rashi and Radak read the king as Hezekiah and the officials as his court. Later Jewish commentators read the outpouring of 32:15 of the messianic age.
views.X: Jerome and most church fathers read the king as Christ and the spirit of 32:15 as the gift of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. The KJV's line in 32:2, "a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind," became a favorite line about Christ as the believer's refuge.
views.F: Futurist readers see 32:1 as the reign of the Messiah on earth, when the land itself is renewed (32:15–18). Premillennial writers place it in the thousand-year kingdom; Jewish hope places it in the days of the Messiah.

deep.b:
The passage moves in three steps. First come the rulers: a king who reigns for righteousness and officials who rule for justice, each like shelter from storm and heat (32:1–2). Then the people: eyes that see, ears that listen, minds that understand and tongues that speak plainly (32:3–4), the undoing of the hardening of 6:9–10. Last comes a contrast of character: the godless fool and the crook, with their lies against the poor, beside the noble whose plans and deeds are noble (32:5–8).

The king here is not the main actor, and he has no name or David's title. That has led readers in three directions. Hezekiah: Rashi and Radak, and many modern readers, see the reformer king of chapters 36–39, whose court would replace the men who made treaties with Egypt. An ideal: many critical scholars think of a wisdom poem, describing good government in general, perhaps added when Josiah was king. The Messiah: the church fathers, and Calvin after them, read it of Christ, while Calvin also saw a first, partial fulfillment in Hezekiah.

What the poem stresses is that good rule restores truth. Under bad rulers words lose their meaning (5:20, "those who call evil good"); under a just king a crook is called a crook again.

echoes: Isaiah 9:6–7; Isaiah 11:1–9; Isaiah 6:9–10; Isaiah 3:16–4:1; Isaiah 44:3; Joel 2:28–29; Acts 2:17–18; James 3:18; Proverbs 16:12; Amos 6:1

settings.what: The just king and the noble
settings.by: Isaiah (or, for many scholars, a later wise writer in his tradition)
settings.to: Jerusalem's ruling class and the people who suffered under them
settings.when: in Hezekiah's reign, or (for others) in Josiah's or after the exile
settings.why: To describe what just rule looks like and to set it against the fools and crooks in power. If the hearers were Hezekiah's court, it is a call to reform; if later readers, it is a hope for a king still to come.
views: A promise of reform under Hezekiah (Rashi, Radak, many modern readers).
A portrait of good rule from Josiah's time or later (Barth and others).
A prophecy of Christ's reign (Jerome, Calvin) or of the Messiah (later Jewish readers).

settings.when: probably a year before the harvest failed in the invasion of 701
settings.why: To jolt the women out of their sense of safety and teach them to lament in advance. The women were the ones who sang at harvest festivals, and they are told to wail at a funeral instead.

settings.what: When the spirit is poured out
settings.by: Isaiah, or a later voice continuing his words
settings.to: the people of a ruined Judah
settings.when: after the ruin of 32:14, looking to a time when God renews the land
settings.why: To promise that the desolation is not the end: God's spirit will make the wilderness fruitful and fill it with justice and peace. The verses turn the warning to the women into hope for all the people.

title: Who Can Live with the Fire?
sum: The last of Isaiah's six woes turns against the plunderer, the double-crosser who was never betrayed himself. What follows is like a service of worship: the people pray for grace, confess that the LORD fills Zion with justice, and lament that the roads are empty, the treaty broken and the land withered. Then God answers: "Now I will rise up." The enemy's plans are dry grass that their own breath will set on fire.

The sinners in Zion now ask who can live beside that fire, and the answer is a life of justice and honesty. The chapter ends with a vision: the people will see a king in his beauty, the Assyrian officials will be a memory, and Jerusalem will be a tent that is never taken down, guarded by the LORD as by a broad river, a city where no one says "I am sick" and guilt is forgiven.
readings: Read as a liturgy

Since Hermann Gunkel (1924), many have read the chapter as a "prophetic liturgy": a prayer, a lament, God's answer, an entrance liturgy like Psalms 15 and 24, and a promise. Read that way, it was shaped for worship in Jerusalem's temple.
Read as the end of 28–33

The woes that began with Samaria's drunken leaders (28:1) end with the destroyer's ruin and Zion's peace. Read this way, the chapter gathers the themes of 28–32 (false alliances, the broken covenant, the coming king) into one closing vision.

views.H: The plunderer is Assyria, which took Hezekiah's tribute (2 Kings 18:14–16) and then attacked Jerusalem anyway. The empty roads, the weeping envoys and the officials counting towers belong to the siege of 701, and the vision of 33:17–24 to Jerusalem's relief.
views.C: Many scholars date the chapter after Isaiah, even after the exile, because of its psalm-like form and its links with chapters 34–35 and 40–66. Some think it was written to join the first part of the book to what follows. Others, such as J. J. M. Roberts, keep much of it in Isaiah's own setting.
views.J: The Talmud uses 33:15 to show how the prophets summed up the law: Isaiah reduced the commands to six (Bavli Makkot 24a). Jewish commentators differ on whether the king in his beauty (33:17) is Hezekiah, the Messiah or God himself.
views.X: Paul echoes 33:18 in 1 Corinthians 1:20 against human wisdom. The king in his beauty has been read of Christ, and the city where no one is sick and sin is forgiven (33:24) of the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:4). Hebrews 12:29 picks up the fire of God's holiness (33:14).
views.F: Futurist readers see in 33:17–24 the Messiah reigning in Jerusalem, when the city is never again moved and sickness and sin are done away; some link the river of 33:21 with Ezekiel 47 and Zechariah 14:8.

deep.b:
Hermann Gunkel's study of 1924 showed how many voices the chapter has. A woe on the destroyer (33:1) is followed by the community's prayer, "LORD, show us grace" (33:2–4), a hymn-like confession (33:5–6), a lament over the broken treaty and the withered land (33:7–9) and God's reply, "Now I will rise up" (33:10–13). Then comes a question and answer like the entrance liturgies of Psalm 15 and Psalm 24: who may live in God's presence? (33:14–16). The chapter ends in a promise of the king and of Zion secure (33:17–24).

Whether the chapter was ever used in worship is unknown. But its form fits Isaiah's book, where the prophet's words are answered by the people's songs (12:1–6; 25:1–12; 26:1–21).

echoes: Isaiah 21:2; Isaiah 24:16; Psalm 15; Psalm 24:3–6; Psalm 46:4; Psalm 103:3; Isaiah 6:1–5; Isaiah 35:2; 1 Corinthians 1:20; Hebrews 12:29; Revelation 21:4; 2 Kings 18:14–17

settings.to: Jerusalem, hearing judgment pronounced on its enemy
settings.when: when the empire that broke faith has done its worst, most likely Assyria in 701
settings.why: To assure Judah that the destroyer will be destroyed in turn, by the same measure.

settings.by: the community of Jerusalem, in the prophet's words
settings.when: during the siege, with the roads cut and the envoys returning in tears
settings.why: To ask for grace, to confess that the LORD is Zion's real treasure, and to bring the broken treaty and the ruined land before God. Hearing it as prayer shows that the prophet speaks with his people, not only to them.

settings.to: the enemy nations, and "you who live far off" and "you who are near"
settings.when: in answer to the lament
settings.why: To announce that God will now act and that the enemy's plans will burn up. The words are addressed to the nations but heard by Judah as comfort.

settings.what: Who can live with the fire?
settings.by: the sinners in Zion ask; the prophet answers
settings.when: as God's holy presence is revealed in judgment
settings.why: To show that the fire that destroys Assyria also tests Zion, and that only those who live justly can dwell with God. Like the gate liturgy of Psalm 15, it sets the moral terms for entering God's presence.

settings.to: the people of Jerusalem under siege, or (on the later view) readers after it
settings.when: looking past the crisis to a city at peace
settings.why: To promise that the terror of Assyrian officials will be only a memory, that Zion will be secure under the LORD as judge, commander and king, and that sickness and guilt will be gone.
views: A vision of Jerusalem relieved after 701, with the king restored.
A picture of the age to come, written later to close chapters 28–33.

title: The LORD's Sword over Edom
sum: The whole world is called to hear its sentence. The LORD is angry with all the nations and has put their armies under the ban; the mountains run with blood, the army of heaven rots, and the sky rolls up like a scroll. Then the sword comes down on Edom, Judah's neighbor and old enemy, in a slaughter pictured as a vast sacrifice at Bozrah.

It is the LORD's day of vengeance, to win Zion's case. Edom burns like Sodom, and its land is measured out not for building but for chaos, the "shapeless and empty" of Genesis 1:2. Owls, jackals, a goat-demon and Lilith, a night creature of legend, take it over, each with its partner, as the LORD's scroll has written. The chapter is the dark half of a pair: chapter 35 turns the same desert into a garden.
readings: Read as judgment on a real nation

Edom shared in Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC (Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 10–14), and the chapter announces its punishment. Edom did decline: its kingdom ended after the 500s BC, Arab peoples moved into its land, and many Edomites moved west into southern Judah.
Read as a picture of the end

The cosmic language, the whole army of heaven rotting and the sky rolled up, reaches beyond one nation. Many readers take Edom as the model of every power that sets itself against God, and the chapter as a picture of the final judgment, as Revelation uses it.

views.H: Edom's hostility to Judah is old, and Isaiah already names it (21:11–12). Its fall came in stages: Babylon's campaigns (Nabonidus marched through Edom about 552 BC), the coming of Arab tribes, and its people moving into the Negev, where they were later known as Idumeans.
views.C: Most scholars date chapters 34–35 after 586 BC and see them as a later bridge between Isaiah 1–33 and 40–66, close in style to 63:1–6 and to Second Isaiah. The "LORD's scroll" (34:16) is often read as the book of Isaiah itself, already being studied.
views.J: In rabbinic tradition Edom came to stand for Rome, and later for Christian Europe. Medieval commentators such as Radak read the chapter as the downfall of Rome at the coming of the Messiah.
views.X: Revelation borrows the chapter for the end of the world (Revelation 6:13–14) and for Babylon's fall (Revelation 18:2; 19:3). Many church writers read Edom as the world opposed to Christ, and the day of vengeance as the last judgment.
views.F: Futurist and dispensational readers place the chapter at the close of the great tribulation, linking Bozrah with 63:1–6, where the Messiah comes from Edom in garments stained red, and the cosmic signs with Matthew 24:29.

deep.h: 34:4 and the end of the world
deep.b:
Isaiah 34:4 is one of the sources of the Bible's picture of the end. Revelation's sixth seal echoes it: "The stars of the sky fell to the earth, the way a fig tree drops its unripe figs when a strong wind shakes it" and "The sky pulled away like a scroll as it rolls up" (Revelation 6:13–14). Jesus' words about the last days, "the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken" (Matthew 24:29), draw on 13:10 and on the Greek of this verse, which has "all the powers of the heavens will melt." 2 Peter 3:10–12 speaks of the heavens dissolving with fire.

Literal. Many readers take these passages as describing a real undoing of the heavens at the end, before a new heaven and earth (65:17; Revelation 21:1). Symbolic. Others, from Calvin to many modern scholars, note that Isaiah uses the same language for the fall of Babylon (13:10) and Edom, and read it as the prophets' way of saying that a political world is collapsing. Both. A third view sees each historical judgment as a preview of the final one, so the words are fulfilled in stages.

deep.h: The Great Isaiah Scroll's two halves
deep.b:
In the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), column 27 ends with 33:24 followed by three blank lines, and chapter 34 begins at the top of column 28. The handwriting and spelling of the second half differ somewhat from the first. Emanuel Tov and others think two scribes shared the work; others think one scribe worked in two stages. In the second half there are also more gaps that later hands filled in, among them the end of 34:17 into 35:2, 37:5–7 and 38:20–22. Drew Longacre has argued that the copyist was working from a damaged master copy and left spaces where it could not be read.

The break at chapter 33 has interested scholars because it falls almost exactly at the middle of the book. It suggests that some ancient copyists treated Isaiah as a book in two halves, though not at the line between 39 and 40 where modern scholars divide it.

echoes: Isaiah 63:1–6; Isaiah 13:10; Isaiah 21:11–12; Obadiah 1–21; Psalm 137:7; Jeremiah 49:7–22; Genesis 1:2; Genesis 19:24; Revelation 6:13–14; Revelation 14:11; Revelation 18:2; Revelation 19:3; Matthew 24:29; Malachi 1:2–4

settings.what: Judgment on the nations and on Edom
settings.by: the prophet, speaking for the LORD
settings.to: the nations of the world in form; in fact Judah and Jerusalem, who heard Edom condemned
settings.when: most likely after 586 BC, when Edom had joined in Jerusalem's ruin; for traditional readers, Isaiah looking ahead
settings.why: To assure Zion that God will take up its case against those who gloated over its fall, and to show that God's judgment reaches the whole created order. For a people who had lost their city, the promise that the LORD would "win Zion's case" (34:8) meant their suffering was seen.
views: Most critical scholars: a poem for Judah after the fall of Jerusalem, when Edom's betrayal was fresh.
Traditional readers: Isaiah foresees Edom's judgment, as he did in 21:11–12, with Edom standing for all God's enemies.

traditions.q: Does "its smoke will keep going up forever" (34:10), which Revelation applies to the lost (Revelation 14:11), describe endless conscious punishment?
views: Hell is real and eternal; its chief pain is eternal separation from God (Catechism 1033–1035). Catholic commentators often read Isaiah's picture of Edom as a type of that judgment.
Punishment is everlasting; many Orthodox writers describe it as God's own fiery presence felt as torment by those who refuse his love.
Yes. The wicked "shall be cast into eternal torments, and be punished with everlasting destruction" (Westminster Confession 33.2); Revelation's use of the verse is read that way.
Divided. Many hold the traditional view; John Stott leaned toward final destruction, and a Church of England report (1995) described hell as total non-being.
No. The wicked are destroyed in the final fire; "forever" describes a result that cannot be undone, as Edom's burning land in 34:10–15 becomes a home for animals.
No. The lost are destroyed forever; there is no place of conscious torment.

title: The Desert in Bloom
sum: After the burning desert of Edom comes its opposite. The wilderness rejoices and blooms like the crocus; the glory of Lebanon, Carmel and Sharon, which withered in 33:9, is given to the desert, and it sees the LORD's glory. The weak and the frightened are told to strengthen their slack hands and wobbling knees and to take heart: "Look, your God!" He is coming himself to save them, and his vengeance on their enemies is their rescue.

Then the blind will see and the deaf hear, the lame will leap like deer and the mute will sing, and water will break out in the wilderness. Through the desert runs a raised road, the Holy Road, safe from lions and open to the redeemed. The ransomed of the LORD will come home to Zion singing, and grief and groaning will run away. The last verse returns word for word in 51:11.
readings: Read as the return from exile

The road through the wilderness and the ransomed coming home to Zion match the return from Babylon promised in 40:3–11 and 51:9–11. Read this way, chapter 35 is a preview of the second half of the book.
Read as a new creation

The desert turned to garden, the healing of bodies and the end of sorrow reach beyond any one return. Jesus pointed to 35:5–6 as signs that God's kingdom had arrived (Matthew 11:5), and Christians have read the chapter as a picture of the renewed world.

views.H: The chapter's road home and its healed travelers fit the return of exiles from Babylon after 539 BC. Some see a promise from Isaiah's time for the scattered people of the northern kingdom and of Judah after 701.
views.C: Most scholars see chapter 35 as later than Isaiah of Jerusalem and close to chapters 40–55 in themes and words. Odil Hannes Steck argued that it was written as a bridge joining the two halves of the book, and that 35:10 was taken from 51:11 for that purpose.
views.J: Jewish tradition reads the chapter of the final redemption and the ingathering of the exiles. The rabbis drew on 35:5–6 to teach that those who are raised will rise with their defects and then be healed, so that all will know they are the same people (Genesis Rabbah 95:1).
views.X: Jesus answered John the Baptist's question with the signs of 35:5–6 and 61:1 (Matthew 11:4–5), and Mark 7:32–37 uses the rare word of the Greek of 35:6. The church has read the Holy Road as the way of salvation, and the early Christians called their faith "the Way" (Acts 9:2).
views.F: Futurist readers expect a literal renewal of the land of Israel, the healing of every disability and a highway to Jerusalem in the messianic kingdom, as in 11:16 and 19:23.

deep.b:
When John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether Jesus was "the one who is coming," Jesus answered with a list: "The blind see again and the lame walk. People with skin disease are made clean and the deaf hear. The dead are raised, and the poor are told the good news" (Matthew 11:5). The list joins 35:5–6 with 26:19, 29:18–19 and 61:1, and it lets John draw the conclusion himself.

A Qumran text, the Messianic Apocalypse (4Q521), shows that some Jews already linked such signs with God's anointed. It speaks of God freeing captives, giving sight to the blind, raising up those bowed down, healing the wounded, making the dead live and bringing good news to the poor. Like Matthew 11:5, it adds the raising of the dead, which Isaiah 35 does not mention, and the good news for the poor from 61:1. Many scholars think Jesus' answer drew on the same way of reading Isaiah.

In Isaiah the healings also reverse the book's own story: the people God made blind and deaf in 6:10 are healed, as 29:18 and 32:3–4 promised. Matthew 15:30–31 and Mark 7:37 describe the crowds seeing these promises happen.

echoes: Isaiah 33:9; Isaiah 40:3–11; Isaiah 51:11; Isaiah 29:18; Isaiah 32:3–4; Isaiah 61:1; Matthew 11:4–6; Matthew 15:30–31; Mark 7:32–37; Acts 3:8; Hebrews 12:12–13; Isaiah 11:16; Isaiah 62:10

settings.what: The desert in bloom and the road home
settings.to: God's people in exile or scattered, weak and afraid
settings.when: after the judgment of chapter 34; for most scholars in the time of the exile, for traditional readers Isaiah looking ahead
settings.why: To give courage to people with "slack hands" and pounding hearts by showing them God coming to save, the land renewed and the road home open. For exiles in Babylon the promise of a safe road through the desert was the promise of home.
views: Written with chapters 40–55 in view, to join the two halves of the book (Steck and many others).
Isaiah sounds the themes he will develop in the later chapters (traditional view).

title: The Rabshakeh at the Wall
sum: In Hezekiah's fourteenth year Sennacherib takes the walled towns of Judah. From Lachish he sends his chief officer, the Rabshakeh, with an army to Jerusalem. He stands where Isaiah once met Ahaz (7:3) and taunts Hezekiah's officials: what is this trust of yours? Egypt is a crushed reed, Judah has no riders for two thousand horses, and the LORD himself sent Assyria against the land.

When the officials beg him to speak Aramaic, he shouts in Hebrew to the men on the wall: Hezekiah cannot save you, and no god has saved any land from the king of Assyria. Make peace with him, and he will take you to a land like your own. The people stay silent, as the king commanded, and the officials bring the speech to Hezekiah with their clothes torn. The chapter follows 2 Kings 18:13–37 almost word for word.
readings: Read as history

The speech fits what we know of Assyrian practice: officers who spoke the local language, appeals over the heads of rulers, promises of deportation to a good land. Sennacherib's annals and the Lachish reliefs confirm the campaign of 701 BC.
Read as Isaiah's book

Placed after chapters 28–35, the Rabshakeh's speech puts the book's question in an enemy's mouth: whom do you trust? Egypt (30:1–7; 31:1–3) or the LORD (30:15)? The answer comes in Hezekiah's prayer and the rescue of chapter 37.

views.H: The campaign of 701 is one of the best documented events in the Bible's history. Sennacherib's own annals list 46 walled towns taken and Hezekiah shut up in Jerusalem, and his palace reliefs show the fall of Lachish. Isaiah does not record the tribute Hezekiah paid (2 Kings 18:14–16).
views.C: Most scholars think chapters 36–39 were taken from Kings and placed here to close the first half of Isaiah, though some, such as Christopher Seitz, argue they were written for Isaiah first. In either case Isaiah's version leaves out Hezekiah's surrender, so his trust is unbroken.
views.J: The rabbis praised Hezekiah's faith and saw in the Rabshakeh a blasphemer. The Talmud tells that the Rabshakeh was an Israelite apostate, which explains his perfect Hebrew (Bavli Sanhedrin 60a).
views.X: Christian readers have seen in the Rabshakeh's speech the tempter's voice, which mixes truth and lies to shake faith (compare Matthew 4:1–11). The officials' silence was praised as the right answer to mockery.
views.F: Some futurist writers see in Sennacherib a pattern of the last enemy who besieges Jerusalem (Zechariah 12–14), and in the rescue a pattern of the final deliverance.

deep.b:
Most of these chapters are the same Hebrew as 2 Kings 18:13–20:19, and this translation uses the same English wherever the Hebrew agrees, including the line breaks of the poem in 37:22–35. The differences are of three kinds.

What Isaiah leaves out. The largest is 2 Kings 18:14–16: Hezekiah's message to Lachish, "I have done wrong," and the tribute of silver and gold stripped from the temple. Isaiah also lacks the two other Assyrian officers of 2 Kings 18:17, the healing promise and the third day of 2 Kings 20:5, and Hezekiah's choice between two signs (2 Kings 20:8–10).

What only Isaiah has. Hezekiah's psalm (38:9–20) is found only here.

Order and wording. In Isaiah the fig poultice and Hezekiah's question come after the psalm (38:21–22), not before the sign. Dozens of small differences in wording are listed in the notes and variants, among them "I say" for "you say" (36:5), "LORD of Armies" (37:16), "he heard" for "he again sent" (37:9) and "he was glad" for "he listened" (39:2).

The effect of the differences is to make Hezekiah in Isaiah a model of trust, set against Ahaz in chapter 7. The notes on 2 Kings 18–20 deal with the history; the notes here deal with what is different and with how the chapters work in Isaiah.

deep.h: Sennacherib's annals: the Taylor and Chicago prisms
deep.b:
Sennacherib's account of his third campaign survives on several clay prisms inscribed in Akkadian. The best known are the Taylor Prism, acquired at Nineveh by Colonel Robert Taylor in 1830 and bought by the British Museum in 1855, and the Oriental Institute Prism in Chicago, bought by James Henry Breasted in 1920; a third copy is in the Israel Museum. They date from about 691 and 689 BC.

Sennacherib says that Hezekiah of Judah did not submit, so he besieged and took 46 of his walled towns and countless villages, using ramps, battering rams and sappers, and carried off 200,150 people with their animals. Hezekiah himself he shut up in Jerusalem, his royal city, "like a bird in a cage," with earthworks around it. Judah's captured towns were given to the Philistine kings of Ashdod, Ekron and Gaza. Afterward Hezekiah sent tribute to Nineveh: 30 talents of gold, 800 talents of silver, precious stones, ivory furniture, his daughters and palace women and musicians.

The annals agree with the Bible on the main facts: the towns taken, the siege of Jerusalem, the tribute. They never claim that Jerusalem was taken, and they say nothing of an army lost. Assyrian annals never report defeats, so their silence can be read in more than one way; see the notes on 2 Kings 18:13–14 and 2 Kings 19:35.

Isaiah says only that the Rabshakeh came "from Lachish" (36:2; 37:8). Sennacherib treated the fall of Lachish, Judah's second city, as the high point of the campaign. He had it carved on the walls of a room in his Southwest Palace at Nineveh, excavated by Austen Henry Layard in the late 1840s and now in the British Museum. The reliefs show the walls and towers of Lachish, a siege ramp with battering rams, archers and slingers, defenders falling, captives impaled, and families walking into exile with carts and animals. Sennacherib sits on his throne to receive the plunder, with a caption naming him and the booty of Lachish.

David Ussishkin's excavations at Lachish (1973–1994) found the Assyrian siege ramp, the only Assyrian siege ramp yet excavated, a counter-ramp built by the defenders inside the wall, and a thick layer of destruction (Level III) with arrowheads and sling stones. Together, the reliefs and the site show what "marched on all the walled towns of Judah and seized them" (36:1) meant.

echoes: 2 Kings 18:13–37; 2 Chronicles 32:1–19; Isaiah 7:3; Isaiah 22:15–25; Isaiah 30:1–7; Isaiah 31:1–3; Isaiah 42:3; Isaiah 10:5–15; Isaiah 30:15

settings.what: The invasion and the meeting at the water channel
settings.when: Hezekiah's fourteenth year, as Sennacherib takes Judah's walled towns and sends the Rabshakeh from Lachish
settings.why: To set the scene: Judah's towns are gone, an Assyrian army stands at Jerusalem, and Hezekiah's three officials go out to meet it at the spot where Isaiah once met Ahaz (7:3).
settings.readers: For Isaiah's readers the place itself recalls chapter 7 and sets Hezekiah beside Ahaz as a test of trust.

settings.what: The Rabshakeh's speech to Hezekiah's officials
settings.by: the Rabshakeh, speaking for the king of Assyria
settings.to: Eliakim, Shebna and Joah, Hezekiah's officials, at the water channel of the Upper Pool
settings.when: 701 BC, after the fall of Judah's walled towns, with Lachish under siege
settings.why: To break the will of Judah's leaders by attacking every ground of their confidence: Egypt, their army, the LORD himself. Knowing that it is spoken where Ahaz once refused Isaiah's sign gives the question "What is this trust of yours?" its edge.
settings.readers: For readers of Isaiah the speech restates the book's own question about trust, now from the enemy's side, and prepares for the answer of chapter 37.

settings.what: The officials' plea and the Rabshakeh's reply
settings.by: Eliakim, Shebna and Joah; then the Rabshakeh
settings.to: each other, in the hearing of the men on the wall
settings.when: in the middle of the speech
settings.why: The officials want to keep the talks private; the Rabshakeh refuses, because his real audience is the soldiers who will suffer the siege.

settings.what: The Rabshakeh's speech to the people on the wall
settings.by: the Rabshakeh, in the Judean language
settings.to: the ordinary soldiers and citizens on Jerusalem's wall
settings.when: the same day
settings.why: To split the people from their king by offering peace, food and a good land, and by mocking the LORD as one more powerless god. The offer reflects Assyria's policy of moving conquered peoples.
settings.readers: For Isaiah's readers in exile, the promise of "a land like your own land" had come true in the worst way, and the question of whether the LORD could rescue was their own.

settings.when: at the end of the Rabshakeh's speech
settings.why: The people obey the king and say nothing, and the officials bring the speech to Hezekiah with torn clothes. The scene moves the decision from the wall to the king and, through him, to the LORD.
settings.readers: Readers who knew Isaiah's call to quiet trust (30:15) could see it obeyed here.

title: Hezekiah's Prayer and the Night of the Angel
sum: Hezekiah tears his clothes, goes into the LORD's house and sends his officials to Isaiah: the children have come to birth and there is no strength to deliver them. Isaiah answers that the king of Assyria will hear a report, go home and fall by the sword. Sennacherib sends a letter instead, boasting that no god has saved any land from him. Hezekiah spreads it out before the LORD and prays that every kingdom will know that he alone is the LORD.

Isaiah's answer is a poem: Daughter Zion laughs at the proud king, whose victories were planned by God long ago, and who will be led home with a hook in his nose. A sign of three harvests and a promise follow: he will not shoot an arrow at this city. That night the angel of the LORD strikes the Assyrian camp. Sennacherib goes home to Nineveh, where his sons kill him in his god's temple.
readings: Read as fulfillment

Within Isaiah, the chapter fulfills what the prophet had said in 10:24–34, 14:24–27, 29:5–8 and 31:4–9: Assyria will fall, not by a human sword, and Zion will be spared. The book shows the word of the LORD coming true.
Read as a prayer answered

The turning point is Hezekiah's prayer (37:14–20). Isaiah's answer begins "Because you prayed to me" (37:21), and the poem and the rescue follow. The chapter is the book's great example of a king who trusts and prays instead of making alliances.

views.H: Sennacherib did withdraw without taking Jerusalem, and he was murdered by a son in 681 BC, as the Babylonian Chronicle records. How the withdrawal came about, whether by plague, by news from home or by God's direct act, is discussed in the notes on 2 Kings 19:35.
views.C: Many scholars see two accounts woven together, one ending with a report and a withdrawal (37:7, 37:37–38), the other with the letter, the prayer and the angel. The poem in 37:22–29 may be older material from Isaiah. The story telescopes twenty years between 701 and 681.
views.J: The rabbis placed the angel's blow on Passover night, and the Talmud says God wished to make Hezekiah the Messiah and Sennacherib Gog and Magog, but Hezekiah sang no song after his rescue (Bavli Sanhedrin 94a).
views.X: Christian writers have taken Hezekiah's spreading of the letter before the LORD as a model of prayer in crisis. Lord Byron's "The Destruction of Sennacherib" (1815) made the scene famous in English. The confession that the LORD alone is God (37:20) anticipates the monotheism of 43–46.
views.F: Some futurist readers see in Assyria's sudden fall before Jerusalem a pattern of the final deliverance of the city in the last days (Zechariah 14:3; Revelation 20:9).

deep.h: Herodotus 2.141 and the night of the angel
deep.b:
The Greek historian Herodotus, who traveled in Egypt about 450–440 BC, heard a story there from Egyptian priests. When "Sanacharib, king of the Arabians and Assyrians," marched on Egypt, the priest-king Sethos, whom the warriors had deserted, went into the temple and wept before the god's image. The god told him in a dream that he would send helpers. Sethos marched to Pelusium, at Egypt's border, with an army of traders and craftsmen. In the night, field mice swarmed over the Assyrian camp and gnawed their quivers, bowstrings and shield handles, so that the next day the Assyrians fled without weapons and many fell. A stone statue of the king, holding a mouse, stood in the temple of Hephaestus, with an inscription telling all who saw it to fear the gods.

The story differs from Isaiah's in place, people and means. But both remember a sudden, divine defeat of Sennacherib's army in a single night, after a king's prayer in a temple. Some historians link the mice with plague, as in 1 Samuel 6:4–5; Josephus later describes the event as a plague. Others think the Egyptian and Judean stories grew from the same memory of 701, when Sennacherib withdrew from the west. See the deep section on 2 Kings 19 for the wider question.

echoes: 2 Kings 19:1–37; 2 Chronicles 32:20–23; Isaiah 1:8; Isaiah 10:5–34; Isaiah 14:24–27; Isaiah 29:5–8; Isaiah 31:4–9; Isaiah 9:7; Isaiah 43:10–11; Isaiah 46:9–10; Psalm 46; Exodus 12:23

settings.what: Hezekiah goes to the temple and sends to Isaiah
settings.when: on hearing the Rabshakeh's words
settings.why: The king tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, enters the LORD's house and sends his officials and the senior priests to the prophet. Every step is the opposite of seeking help from Egypt.
settings.readers: For readers of Isaiah, this is the turning to the LORD that 31:6 called for.

settings.by: Hezekiah, through Eliakim, Shebna and the elders of the priests
settings.when: right after the Rabshakeh's speech
settings.why: To admit Judah's helplessness and to ask the prophet to pray for the remnant. In Isaiah's book it is the opposite of Ahaz, who would not ask (7:12).
settings.readers: Isaiah's readers saw a king who did what the book asked: he turned to the LORD's word instead of to Egypt.

settings.when: the same day
settings.why: To tell the king not to be afraid and to announce the outcome in brief: a report, a retreat, a death by the sword at home.

settings.what: The Rabshakeh's return and the news of Tirhakah
settings.when: after Lachish, with the Assyrian king fighting at Libnah
settings.why: To show the first part of Isaiah's word coming true: a report reaches the king (37:7). The news of Tirhakah's march sets off a second threat, the letter.

settings.when: when news came that Tirhakah of Cush was marching
settings.why: To keep Hezekiah from relying on the LORD while Assyria dealt with Egypt, by listing the gods and kings Assyria had already destroyed.

settings.what: Hezekiah spreads the letter before the LORD
settings.when: on receiving Sennacherib's letter
settings.why: The king reads the letter, goes up to the temple and spreads it out before the LORD, then prays. The gesture puts the enemy's words in front of the one they insult.
settings.readers: For readers in exile, it showed where to take the taunts of empires.

settings.to: the LORD of Armies, in the temple
settings.when: with the Assyrian letter spread out before the LORD
settings.why: To ask for rescue, not for Judah's sake alone, but so that every kingdom on earth will know that the LORD alone is God. The prayer turns the insult to the living God into a reason for God to act.
settings.readers: For readers in exile, among the gods of Babylon, the prayer's contrast between the living God and idols of wood and stone was the message of chapters 40–48.

settings.to: Sennacherib, addressed in the poem; heard by Hezekiah
settings.when: in answer to the prayer
settings.why: To mock the Assyrian king's boasts and to reveal that his conquests were God's plan, and that God will now lead him home. Daughter Zion's laughter turns the siege upside down.

settings.when: in the same answer
settings.why: To give a sign that will confirm the rescue over three years of harvests, to promise a remnant, and to declare that the Assyrian will not enter the city or shoot an arrow at it.

settings.when: the end of the campaign of 701, and twenty years later
settings.why: To show the word of the LORD fulfilled in every point: the army struck, the king gone home, and his death by the sword in his own god's house.
settings.readers: For Isaiah's later readers the story was proof that the LORD could defend Zion, and the problem of why he did not do so in 586.

title: Hezekiah's Sickness and His Song
sum: Hezekiah falls ill, and Isaiah tells him to set his house in order: he will die. The king turns his face to the wall and prays with tears, and the LORD sends Isaiah back with a new word. Fifteen years will be added to his life, and the city will be rescued from Assyria. As a sign, the shadow on the steps of Ahaz goes back ten steps.

Then comes a psalm Hezekiah wrote after his recovery, found only in Isaiah. He remembers feeling his life pulled up like a tent and cut off like cloth from a loom, chirping like a bird, crushed as by a lion. Then the turn: God loved him out of the pit and threw his sins behind his back. The dead in Sheol cannot praise God; the living can, and they will sing at the LORD's house. Last come the fig poultice and the king's question about the sign.
readings: Read as a king's story
Hezekiah's illness is a personal crisis set inside the national one, and his prayer is answered as his prayer for the city was in chapter 37. The book shows a king whose trust is rewarded.
Read as Jerusalem's story

Many readers see Hezekiah as a picture of Zion itself: sick to death, given new life, singing God's praise in the temple. The psalm then becomes the song of a people who came through the edge of death.

views.H: The illness came before the Assyrian threat ended (38:6). Its date is debated. If Hezekiah came to the throne in 715, his fourteenth year is 701 and the fifteen added years fill out his 29-year reign; if he came to the throne about 729/727, as 2 Kings 18:1, 9–10 suggest, the illness falls about 714–711. Manasseh became king at twelve (2 Kings 21:1), so, if there was no co-regency, he was born in the third of the added years.
views.C: Many scholars think the psalm was written later and placed in Hezekiah's mouth, as psalms are given to Hannah (1 Samuel 2) and Jonah (Jonah 2). Its absence from Kings, and the disorder of 38:21–22, suggest that Isaiah's version of the chapter was reworked, perhaps after the Kings version.
views.J: The Talmud says Hezekiah was condemned because he had not married and had children, foreseeing that his sons would be wicked; after his repentance he married and fathered Manasseh (Bavli Berakhot 10a). The Talmud also says he prayed "from the chambers of his heart" (Bavli Berakhot 10b).
views.X: The psalm entered the church's prayer: the Greek Psalter adds it to its biblical songs, and the Roman Liturgy of the Hours sings it at Morning Prayer and in the Office of the Dead. Christian readers hear in God casting sins behind his back the forgiveness of the gospel.
views.F: Futurist readers see little in the chapter that is still to come. Some read the turning back of the sun as a preview of God's power over time and creation at the end (Joshua 10:12–14; Revelation 21:23).

deep.b:
The sign is told more briefly in Isaiah than in Kings: God announces it, without Hezekiah's choice, and "the sun went back ten steps." The Hebrew says ma'alot, "steps," five times. What were they? A stairway. Many think of an outdoor staircase built by Ahaz, perhaps to the roof chamber of 2 Kings 23:12, on which the shadow of a wall crept down as the sun rose higher, or up as it set; the Great Isaiah Scroll reads "the steps of the upper room of Ahaz." A shadow clock. Others think of a sundial with steps, like Egyptian shadow clocks; the KJV's "sun dial of Ahaz" reflects this view.

As for the event, three readings are common. A miracle. The sign is God's direct act, like the sun standing still for Joshua (Joshua 10:12–14); 2 Chronicles 32:31 says Babylon's envoys came to ask about "the sign that had happened in the land," and Ben Sira praised it (Sirach 48:23). A natural cause. Some have proposed a partial eclipse or an unusual refraction of light, affecting only the shadow on the steps. A sign story. Others read it as a story told to show that the God who gives life also rules time. All agree that the point is God's answer to Hezekiah's prayer.

The psalm is a song of thanksgiving after illness, like Psalms 30 and 116. It moves from lament, remembered (38:10–14), to the turn when God acts (38:15–17), and to praise in the temple (38:18–20). Its pictures are vivid: the gates of Sheol, a herder's tent pulled up, a weaver cutting finished cloth from the loom, a lion breaking bones, the thin cries of swifts and doves, and the plea, "put up the bond for me." Several verses (38:11, 38:14–16) are among the hardest Hebrew in the book.

Was it Hezekiah's? The heading says so, and Hezekiah's court is linked with collecting songs and wise sayings (Proverbs 25:1; 2 Chronicles 29:30). Many scholars think the psalm was composed for temple worship and later placed here, as Hannah's and Jonah's songs were placed in their stories. Either way, in Isaiah it tells how the king understood what happened: not a cure alone but forgiveness and a new life given for praise.

The psalm lived on in worship. The Greek Psalter added it to its collection of biblical songs as the Prayer of Hezekiah, and the Roman Liturgy of the Hours sings 38:10–14 and 38:17–20 at Morning Prayer and in the Office of the Dead.

echoes: 2 Kings 20:1–11; 2 Chronicles 32:24–26; Psalm 6:5; Psalm 30:9; Psalm 88:10–12; Psalm 102:24; Psalm 103:3; Psalm 115:17; Job 7:6; Job 17:3; Matthew 16:18; Joshua 10:12–14; Isaiah 33:24

settings.when: "in those days," probably before or during the Assyrian crisis
settings.why: To tell the king to prepare his household for his death. The blunt word is the occasion for the prayer that changes it.

settings.to: the LORD, with his face to the wall
settings.when: on hearing the sentence
settings.why: To ask God to remember his faithful life. The prayer is short and tearful, and God answers it at once.
settings.readers: For Isaiah's readers it showed a king whose prayer could change a sentence, as Jerusalem's would in 40:1–2.

settings.what: The new word and the sign
settings.when: after the prayer
settings.why: To add fifteen years, to promise rescue from Assyria and to confirm both with the shadow going back on Ahaz's steps.

settings.by: Hezekiah, as the heading presents it
settings.to: the LORD; and the worshipers who will sing it at the LORD's house
settings.when: after his recovery
settings.why: To give thanks by telling the story of his near death and rescue, and to promise lifelong praise in the temple. The shift to "we" in 38:20 shows the song was meant for others to sing.
views: Written by the king after his recovery, as the heading says, perhaps for use in the temple he restored.
A thanksgiving psalm composed later and set in Hezekiah's story (many critical scholars).

settings.what: The figs and the king's question
settings.when: before the healing, though told after the psalm
settings.why: To record the remedy and the request for a sign that appear earlier in 2 Kings 20:7–8. Their place here is discussed in the note and variant.

traditions.q: Hezekiah says "It is not Sheol that thanks you" (38:18). Are the dead conscious between death and the resurrection?
views: Yes. Each soul is judged at death and goes to heaven, to purification or to hell, awaiting the resurrection (Catechism 1021–1022, 1030). Hezekiah speaks from before the full revelation of life after death.
Yes. Before Christ the dead were held in Hades; Christ broke its gates, and the departed are alive in God, for whom the church prays.

Believers who die are with Christ. Luther often spoke of death as a deep sleep from which the faithful wake at the last day as if after a moment, yet he held that the soul lives before God; Lutherans reject purgatory.
Yes. The souls of believers at death are made perfect and pass into glory (Westminster Confession 32.1); the verse means the dead no longer praise God among the living.
No. Death is an unconscious sleep until the resurrection, and texts like 38:18, Psalm 115:17 and Ecclesiastes 9:5 are read as plain teaching (Fundamental Beliefs 26).
No. Sheol is the common grave of mankind, and the dead are conscious of nothing until God raises them.

title: Envoys from Babylon
sum: Merodach-baladan, king of Babylon, sends letters and a gift to Hezekiah after his recovery. Hezekiah, glad of the attention, shows the envoys everything: silver and gold, spices and oil, his armory, all his storehouses. Isaiah comes and asks who these men were and where they came from. "From a land far away," the king answers, "from Babylon," and he admits there was nothing in his house or storerooms he did not let them see.

Isaiah then speaks the LORD's word: the days are coming when all of it will be carried off to Babylon, and some of Hezekiah's own descendants will serve as eunuchs in the Babylonian king's palace. Hezekiah answers that the word is good, for there will be peace and safety in his own days. With that, the story of Hezekiah ends, and the book's next words are "Comfort, comfort my people."
readings: Read as a warning

Hezekiah, so faithful in chapters 36–38, now trusts a foreign alliance and shows off his wealth. Read this way, the chapter shows that even the best of kings failed, and that Judah's trust in nations would end in exile.
Read as a hinge

The chapter turns the book from Assyria to Babylon. Babylon, a small ally here, will become the power that takes Judah away, and chapters 40–55 speak to the exiles there. Read this way, chapter 39 is the door into the second half of Isaiah.

views.H: Marduk-apla-iddina II ruled Babylon in 721–710 BC and again for some months in 703, and he looked for allies against Assyria. The embassy's date depends on Hezekiah's: about 703, when Hezekiah was preparing to revolt against Sennacherib, or about 713–711, in Merodach-baladan's first reign and the years of the Ashdod revolt. Isaiah's word came true in 597 and 586, when Nebuchadnezzar carried off the palace treasures and the royal family (2 Kings 24:13–15).
views.C: Most scholars think the prophecy of exile to Babylon was written or sharpened after the events, and that the chapter was placed here, out of time order, to lead into chapters 40–55. Peter Ackroyd and Christopher Seitz argued that chapters 36–39 were shaped to serve as this bridge.
views.J: The Talmud reads the eunuchs of 39:7 as Daniel and his companions (Bavli Sanhedrin 93b). The rabbis often found Hezekiah's fault in pride, in showing God's gifts to foreigners as if they were his own.
views.X: Christian commentators have usually found in Hezekiah a warning against pride after God's blessing (2 Chronicles 32:25). Some read his last words as selfish relief, others as humble acceptance of God's judgment, as in 1 Samuel 3:18.
views.F: Some futurist readers see Babylon here as the first appearance of the power that Revelation 17–18 calls "Babylon the Great," the last enemy of God's people.

deep.b:
Marduk-apla-iddina II ("Marduk has given an heir") was a leader of the Chaldean tribe of Bit-Yakin in the marshes of southern Babylonia. With help from Elam he seized Babylon in 721 BC, the year Sargon II came to Assyria's throne, and held it until Sargon drove him out in 710. When Sargon died in battle in 705, Babylon revolted again, and Marduk-apla-iddina returned in 703 for some months, until Sennacherib defeated him in his first campaign. He fled to Elam and died there. Assyrian records describe him as a persistent rebel. Isaiah spells his name "Merodach-baladan," closer to the Babylonian than Kings' "Berodach-baladan."

Whether the embassy came about 703, when Hezekiah was preparing to stop paying tribute to Assyria (2 Kings 18:7), or about 713–711, when the Ashdod revolt was drawing in Judah, a letter and a gift from such a man were surely about more than his health. Showing the envoys the arsenal (39:2) suggests talks about a joint revolt, east and west at once. That explains Isaiah's anger. He had warned against trusting Egypt (30:1–7; 31:1–3); trusting Babylon was no better.

The chapter is placed after the rescue of 701 although it happened before it. In the book's order, the Assyrian crisis ends in chapter 37, and Babylon enters in chapter 39. The next chapter speaks to Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile: "Comfort, comfort my people, / your God says" (40:1).

echoes: 2 Kings 20:12–19; 2 Chronicles 32:25–31; Isaiah 13:5; Isaiah 21:9; Isaiah 33:6; Isaiah 40:1–2; Isaiah 56:3–5; 2 Kings 24:13–15; Daniel 1:3–7; 1 Samuel 3:18

settings.when: after Hezekiah's recovery; about 703 BC or about 713–711, depending on the chronology
settings.why: Merodach-baladan sends letters and a gift, and Hezekiah, glad of the attention, shows the envoys all his treasures and his arsenal. The scene sets up the oracle: what he showed off will be carried to Babylon.
settings.readers: For readers after 586, the scene explained how the treasures of Jerusalem came to be in Babylon, and why.

settings.when: right after the Babylonian envoys' visit, about 703 BC or about 713–711 (the date is debated)
settings.why: Isaiah's questions draw out what Hezekiah has done, so that the king condemns himself in his own words: "there was not a thing I didn't show them."

settings.what: The oracle of exile to Babylon
settings.by: Isaiah, speaking for the LORD of Armies
settings.when: the same visit
settings.why: To announce that the treasures he showed off and some of his own descendants will be carried to Babylon. For readers who had lived through 586, it explained the exile as foretold and deserved.
settings.readers: For the book's readers in or after the exile, the oracle ties their present to the story of Hezekiah and opens the way to the comfort of chapter 40.
views: Isaiah foresaw the exile more than a century ahead (traditional view).
The prophecy was written or sharpened after 586 (most critical scholars).

settings.when: after the oracle
settings.why: To accept the word as good, adding that there will be peace in his own days. Whether the words show relief, selfishness or humble acceptance is debated; see the note.
